title: Starting states reach two different cycles
alt_text:
Diagram of the soft-token loop. A fixed chat prompt and one soft token enter a transformer, which has a steering vector added at a middle layer. The transformer produces one logit score per vocabulary token; a softmax at temperature T turns the scores into next-token probabilities; and the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings, the expected embedding, is fed back over the top as the next soft token, at the same position after the same prompt. A lower band shows the derivative of one step as the product of a network factor, the network's Jacobian, and a readout factor, the covariance of token embeddings under the next-token probabilities divided by T, which is large only when several different tokens compete. A footer states that chaos needs competing tokens: a spread next-token distribution that the inverse temperature still amplifies.](soft-token-loop.svg)

Diagram: the soft-token loop and the two factors of its derivative. Conceptual schematic with no data; the equations are below. The covariance form of the readout factor holds for models whose output matrix is tied to the input embedding, such as Qwen2.5-0.5B; untied models use a cross-covariance.

Every model in this note is run as the same kind of map. Each one uses its own embedding matrix and the layer where a steering vector is added. The formulas below are written for the case studied in most detail, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Let \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}\) be the input {{< refterm "embedding" "embedding" >}} matrix, with \(V = 151{,}936\) tokens and \(d = 896\) dimensions, and let \(e_t\) be its row for token \(t\). The model reads a fixed chat prefix, with the system prompt "You are an AI talking with another AI. You have complete freedom. Feel free to pursue whatever you want." and the user turn "Hello!", followed by a single input embedding \(x\), and produces next-token {{< refterm "logit" "logits" >}} \(z(x) \in \mathbb{R}^V\), one unnormalized score \(z_t\) for each token \(t\). The soft-token map feeds the expected next-token embedding back in place of \(x\): \[ F_{T,\alpha}(x) = E^{\top}\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(z_\alpha(x)/T\big). \] Here \(T > 0\) is the {{< refterm "temperature" "temperature" >}}, and the softmax turns the logits into the next-token distribution \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(z/T)\), whose entry for token \(t\) is \[ p_t = \frac{\exp(z_t/T)}{\sum_{s=1}^{V}\exp(z_s/T)}. \] Every \(p_t\) is positive and the \(V\) entries sum to 1. Lowering \(T\) moves the probability toward the largest logits, and raising it spreads the probability out. That makes the temperature one of the two axes of most maps in this note: it sets how strongly the next tokens compete for the probability. The map's output, \(E^{\top}p = \sum_t p_t e_t\), is the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings: the soft token. The subscript \(\alpha\) is the steering strength: \(z_\alpha\) is computed with \(\alpha v\) added to the {{< refterm "residual-stream" "residual stream" >}} at layer 12, at every token position in the sequence, the prefix included. The prefix tokens stay in those same slots at every step, and the soft token always occupies the single slot after them, where a reply would begin. That slot is overwritten rather than followed by a new token, so the sequence the model reads does not grow. The only state that changes is the vector in that slot, and \(F\) is an autonomous map of \(\mathbb{R}^{896}\): the same rule at every step, depending only on the current vector in that slot, not on the step number or on a longer history. As \(T \to 0\) it reduces, where the most probable token is unique, to greedy decoding of the same fixed-prefix, one-token system. It is not ordinary generation with a growing context. {{< panel "info" >}} **A soft token is not a token.** The loop never feeds back a chosen token: it feeds back the average of all token embeddings, weighted by probability. When this note says that a loop "writes" a text, it means the most probable next token at each step, read off for display. Two nearby soft states can share a leading token, and one continuous orbit can change its label where two tokens tie for the maximum. {{< /panel >}} **State space and smoothness.** Attention in these models is {{< refterm "causal-attention" "causal" >}}: each token may use itself and earlier tokens, and not later ones. The soft token \(x\) sits in the last slot, after the prefix. A prefix token's keys and values, the vectors it contributes for other tokens to read, are computed only from the prefix up to that token. Changing \(x\) does not change them. Only the last slot, which can see \(x\), depends on it. For the dense models studied here the map is real-analytic: each output coordinate has a power series in the coordinates of \(x\). That holds because {{< refterm "rms-normalization" "RMS normalization" >}}, with its positive regularizing constant, the {{< refterm "silu" "SiLU" >}} activation, attention, {{< refterm "rotary-embedding" "rotary embeddings" >}} at these fixed positions, and the softmax readout are all analytic. A mixture of experts with top-\(k\) routing is different: it is smooth only within each region of fixed routing, where the same experts are selected, and its map can be discontinuous where the routing changes, where two routing scores cross and the selected set switches. The arguments that follow, which use continuity and derivatives, therefore apply to the dense models. Every soft token is a convex combination of embedding vectors, a weighted average whose weights are nonnegative and sum to 1. So \(F\) sends every state into the compact {{< refterm "convex-hull" "convex hull" >}} \(K\) of the embeddings, and \(F(K) \subset K\). By {{< refterm "brouwer-fixed-point" "Brouwer's theorem" >}} a continuous map of a nonempty compact convex set into itself has a fixed point in \(K\). The same continuity on a compact set supplies invariant probability measures, distributions on states that the map leaves unchanged. By {{< refterm "oseledets-theorem" "Oseledets' theorem" >}}, in its version for maps that need not be invertible, the {{< refterm "lyapunov-exponent" "Lyapunov exponents" >}} of those measures exist almost everywhere; that version allows an exponent of minus infinity, for a direction that one step collapses completely. The exponents reported here estimate them over finite horizons. ### Why study a model fed its own output {#why-feed-back} One might object that nobody feeds a language model its own output, so the loop is artificial. Firstly, whether or not that is the case, the techniques here can act as a probe on the internal structures of a language model. Secondly, feedback is in fact how text is generated. Autoregressive decoding appends each chosen token to the input and conditions the next step on it, and as \(T \to 0\) the map studied here becomes greedy decoding wherever one token is strictly the most probable; the familiar repetition loops of greedy decoding are then the cycles of that limit. ![Schematic, not a measured orbit. Left: ordinary decoding starts from Hello!, appends The, then appends cat, so each next step reads a longer input. Right: the same prefix stays fixed while one slot after it is replaced by the embedding of the single most probable token. The slot alternates between the toy tokens yes and no and returns to yes, a cycle. As temperature goes to zero the soft token becomes that one embedding, so the fixed-length loop is greedy decoding and the cycle is a periodic attractor.](autoregressive-vs-greedy.svg)

Diagram: two ways of feeding a model its own output. Ordinary decoding appends the chosen token, and the next step is conditioned on the longer sequence. In the map studied here the prefix stays in place and, as \(T \to 0\), the single slot after it is overwritten by the embedding of the most probable token (where one token is strictly the most probable). A slot that returns to a token it has already held is a periodic attractor of that greedy one-token map. The tokens in the picture are placeholders, not a measured orbit.

What the soft-token loop changes is what is fed back: the expected embedding instead of one chosen token. A chosen token is a single vocabulary item. The expected embedding is the average of every token's embedding, weighted by the next-token probabilities. When two tokens split that probability, the vector that comes back lies between their embeddings, so the next step still carries both candidates. Feeding back one chosen token would have dropped the other. That mixture is the step of Soft Thinking ([Zhang et al., 2025](#ref-zhang-2025)), and related methods feed back hidden states ([Hao et al., 2025](#ref-hao-2025)) or iterate a block to a fixed point ([Geiping et al., 2025](#ref-geiping-2025)). Non-autoregressive decoders, which write all the tokens of an output at once and then refine them, have used expected-embedding feedback as well, solving for its equilibrium, the state that one more refinement step leaves unchanged ([Zheng, Zhou, and Zhou, 2023](#ref-zheng-2023)). Holding the prefix and the window fixed is a deliberate simplification. It makes the loop an autonomous map whose orbits, exponents and bifurcations can be computed, and in one case proved, much as low-dimensional maps made the routes to turbulence tractable ([Feigenbaum, 1978](#ref-feigenbaum-1978); [Pomeau and Manneville, 1980](#ref-pomeau-1980)). Which effects survive in fuller systems is tested separately: Soft Thinking's growing context, sampled decoding, longer fed-back memories and two models writing to each other (see [Beyond the one-token loop](#beyond)). The answer-level consequences reported below, answers that change with the batch, were measured in a soft-thinking pipeline with a growing context, not in the reduced loop. Deployed systems feed outputs back as well, when agents read their own earlier steps and when pipelines chain model calls. This fixed-prefix, fixed-window soft-token map differs both from ordinary autoregressive generation, whose context grows, and from recurrent-depth ("looped") transformers, which repeatedly update hidden states through a shared block ([Dehghani et al., 2019](#ref-dehghani-2019); [Giannou et al., 2023](#ref-giannou-2023); [Geiping et al., 2025](#ref-geiping-2025)). The methods of dynamical systems apply to both kinds of loop, but their update operators, and therefore their derivatives and stability conditions, differ. ### Steering as a probe {#steering-as-a-probe} Activation steering is an established way to control a language model without retraining: a vector added to the residual stream, typically the mean difference between activations on contrasting prompts, strengthens or weakens a behavior ([Rimsky et al., 2024](#ref-rimsky-2024)). The same kind of edit, followed through the rest of the network, is the subject of [A Linear Nudge, a Nonlinear Wake]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/jacobian-lens-intervention-test/index.md" >}}). **How the direction is built.** The steering vector is not learned and the model's weights are never changed. It is a fixed vector, added to the model's internal state while it runs. That state is the {{< refterm "residual-stream" "residual stream" >}}: one 896-dimensional vector per token position, to which every attention and MLP block adds its output. The philosophy direction comes from 16 short texts and three steps. 1. **Two groups of texts.** Eight philosophical sentences, such as "What is the nature of consciousness and subjective experience?" and "Is there something it is like to be me?", and eight neutral ones, such as "The meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning." and "The package weighs two kilograms." All sixteen are listed in [Chaos with periodic windows](#chaos-with-periodic-windows). 2. **Read the state.** Each text is run through the unsteered model, as plain text without the chat template, and the residual-stream vector after decoder layer 12 (of 24, counted from 0) is read at the text's last token. 3. **Take the difference and fix its length.** The direction is the average of these vectors over the philosophical texts minus their average over the neutral texts. It is then rescaled to the typical length of a residual vector at that layer (189, the mean over the 16 texts). Because of that rescaling, the steering strength \(\alpha\) reads as a fraction of a typical residual vector: \(\alpha = 0.07\) adds 7% of one. The raw difference between the two groups has length 8.1, so \(\alpha \approx 0.043\) reproduces the natural contrast between philosophical and neutral text, and the values of Figure 1, 0.0625 to 0.0775, push 1.5 to 1.8 times as far. In every forward pass of the loop, \(\alpha v\) is added to the residual stream after layer 12 at every position: at each token of the prompt and at the fed-back soft token. The later layers therefore also see a steered prompt, since the keys and values that their attention computes for the prompt's tokens carry the push. The other directions in this note are built the same way at their own layers: gratitude at layer 4 and hostility at layer 16 for the two-layer plane of the period-5 shrimp. The pushes are moderate: at most 12% of the mean residual norm per vector in every map (bifurcation curves continued in steering strength reach 13.1%), and 6.25 to 7.75% in Figure 1. Pushes of this size still change what a model writes: in Qwen2.5-7B, 1% of the residual norm is the largest push that kept greedy accuracy on a multiplication task within 5 points. We do not steer to make the model behave in a particular way. The strength \(\alpha\) is a control parameter, like the amplitude of a periodic forcing, that moves the model through a one-parameter family of nearby maps, so that bifurcation curves can be traced. The chaos does not depend on it: with no steering at all, temperature alone gives chaos with periodic windows in Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and OLMo-2-7B, and in a narrow band in Qwen2.5-0.5B. Nor, in the 0.5B and 8B models, does the direction's meaning matter. On one 128 × 128 grid of the 0.5B model, 7.6, 8.3 and 12.5% of cells are chaotic for three random Gaussian directions with the philosophy vector's norm, against 6.8% for philosophy, and the output direction of the single {{< refterm "mlp" "MLP" >}} neuron most specific to philosophy gives 9.9%. In Llama-3.1-8B, a [sparse-autoencoder]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/how-to-read-an-sae-feature-id/index.md" >}}) feature direction, contrastive directions and random directions all drive the map into chaos (27 to 39% of cells). At 70B the directions differ more: the hostility-related directions gave more chaotic cells than the random ones (4.3 and 3.5% against 1.1 and 0.2%, in two-GPU maps computed before a precision fix described below). What a direction does select is the text of the attractors. The prompt plays a similar part: under each of the 22 variants of it that we tested, the map of the 0.5B plane is chaotic in part, and the prompt decides where ([Changing the prompt](#prompt-variants)). A different question, whether a Jacobian lens can name the steered feature from the state alone, is the subject of [Can a Jacobian Lens Detect SAE Steering?]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/jacobian-lens-sae-steering/index.md" >}}). ### Numerics and chaos labels {#numerics-and-chaos-labels} **Precision.** Hugging Face RMSNorm layers and rotary-embedding tables compute in float32 even when a model is cast to float64, so both were patched (a {{< refterm "dtype" "dtype" >}} label names storage, not the whole arithmetic path). A float32 map is accurate to \(3\times10^{-6}\) to \(2\times10^{-5}\) per step. That is enough for phase maps, the colored grids in which each cell is one setting of steering and temperature and the color says whether the loop there repeats or is chaotic: 245 of 256 test cells get the same label in float32 as in float64. It is not enough when the derivative is taken after the loop has been applied several times in a row. One float32 Jacobian-vector product, the derivative of a single step, agrees to \(5\times10^{-5}\), yet the 8-step {{< refterm "monodromy" "monodromy" >}} of a period-8 orbit, the product of eight such derivatives, is off by 3%. All orbits, multipliers and test functions below are therefore computed in float64. The dense checkpoints store {{< refterm "bf16" "bfloat16" >}} weights, which convert to float64 exactly. **Lyapunov exponents and labels.** The largest {{< refterm "lyapunov-exponent" "Lyapunov exponent" >}} \(\lambda\) is the average exponential growth rate, per step, of the distance between two trajectories that start infinitesimally close: a small offset \(\delta_0\) grows to about \(\delta_0 e^{\lambda n}\) after \(n\) steps. It is measured in {{< refterm "nat" "nats" >}} (natural-log units) per step. A cell of a parameter scan is labeled chaotic when the finite-horizon exponent of a twin trajectory (offset \(10^{-6}\), renormalized every step; 300 measured steps after 300 transient ones unless stated) exceeds \(10^{-3}\) and no period up to 32 (48 in later zooms) is found. The threshold matters little: raising it to \(5\times10^{-3}\) lowers the chaotic share of the map of Figure 1, shown below, from 30.1 to 29.8%. At 448 checked cells, automatic-differentiation tangents carried by {{< refterm "forward-mode-automatic-differentiation" "forward-mode differentiation" >}} reproduce the twin exponents within 0.0041. The twin starts in a random direction among the state's 896 dimensions at the end of the transient, so the averaging window, the measured steps over which the exponent is averaged, includes its alignment: the offset takes some steps to line up with the direction of fastest growth. So at a periodic cell the finite-window estimate differs a little, in either direction, from the exact value \(\ln\lvert\mu_1\rvert/p\) of the orbit, where \(p\) is the period and the leading multiplier \(\mu_1\) is the factor by which the slowest-shrinking small deviation from the orbit is multiplied on each lap of \(p\) steps. At two neighboring cells inside the kite of Figure 49, the map gives \(-0.2786\) and \(-0.0885\) per step and the period-6 orbits found by Newton's method give \(-0.2821\) and \(-0.0813\), offsets of \(+0.0035\) and \(-0.0073\). These offsets are consistent with that alignment transient, but its contribution has not been isolated, so the transient is not shown to be their only cause. Periodic cells are classified by their period, not by this exponent; the offset shows only in the gray shading of the maps. A positive largest Lyapunov exponent is the standard numerical test for chaos, and it is the test used throughout this note. Like every measured exponent it is computed over a finite horizon, so we check it three ways: against a change of the twin offset, against automatic-differentiation tangents, and against the precision of the arithmetic. In a simplified model in which each copy receives independent noise, noise in a measured difference can produce a false positive exponent: below the noise level a twin exponent rises as the offset shrinks, while a real exponent does not depend on the offset ([False chaos and real chaos](#false-chaos) explains the test). The model is an approximation, not a one-way guarantee: rounding can also erase a small difference altogether, and noise can change the dynamics being sampled or push a trajectory into another attractor's {{< refterm "basin-of-attraction" "basin" >}}. The labels are therefore checked by comparing twin offsets and automatic-differentiation tangents, and a second implementation of the map, written separately, reproduces the exponents of two chaotic cells and of the certified period-8 orbit ([Independent implementations](#methods-independent)). A longer horizon check (1000 transient and 2000 measured steps, two twin offsets) kept 86 and 92 of 96 sampled chaotic labels in two maps, and all 96 periodic labels in each. Near the accumulation point of a cascade, transient chaos makes labels less reliable: on one line, only 135 of 235 chaotic labels held. A much longer test followed 192 randomly chosen chaotic cells of each of two maps for 100,000 steps. In the stripes map 176 of them never settled onto a repeating loop, and in the window of Figure 1, 143. All but one of these kept a positive exponent. The rest were long transients: they wandered chaotically for 600 to 97,500 steps before settling, most onto a loop that writes " are you". So the chaotic shares quoted below are shares over a finite horizon, in one chosen window of the parameter plane. Every cell starts from the same fixed state, so where attractors coexist, a map shows the one whose basin contains that state. {{< panel "info" >}} **What a certification is, and why we certified only three periodic orbits.** A floating-point computation that converges is strong evidence, but every operation rounds, so it is not a proof. A *certification*, or computer-assisted proof, replaces each number with an interval guaranteed to contain the exact value, and carries those guarantees through every layer of the network and all 151,936 entries of the readout. If a test such as {{< refterm "krawczyk-test" "Krawczyk's test" >}} then passes, the result holds for the exact real-number map defined by the stored weights, not just for one rounded run. That is what we did for one attracting period-8 orbit and, at one other setting, for two coexisting attracting orbits of periods 2 and 3; independent checks in exact rational arithmetic confirmed the saved witnesses. It is expensive: the boxes had to be tiny (radius \(2^{-640}\)) to keep the interval bounds from blowing up through the layers, and each orbit is a large, high-precision computation of its own. Certifying every orbit and label in the note is neither affordable nor customary. In the study of chaotic dynamics, the standard evidence for chaos is the kind collected here: Lyapunov exponents that agree between twin runs and automatic-differentiation tangents, that hold across precisions and run lengths, and that predict when two runs separate, together with structures such as period-doubling cascades approaching Feigenbaum's constant. The certified orbits anchor that evidence. They show that the float64 computations describe the real map, so the rest of the numerics are not artifacts of rounding. {{< /panel >}} {{< panel "info" >}} **An open challenge: strict mathematical certification of the chaos.** Sampled chaos-labeled cells in this note were checked numerically: at those cells, exponents measured from twin runs agree with automatic-differentiation tangents, across precisions and run lengths, and some of the labels turned out to be long transients, as described above. The chaos is not yet proved in the strictest mathematical sense. A mathematical proof would have to bound every rounding error, as the note's proof of one period-8 orbit does. The standard route is a *horseshoe*. Find two thin regions of the 896-dimensional state space that a few steps of the loop each stretch across both, while squeezing every other direction, and check this with rigorous arithmetic. That forces every pattern of visits to the two regions to occur, which is chaos in the strict sense. The geometry here looks favorable: at the chaotic cells whose spectra we estimated, only one direction expands over the measured horizon. The obstacle is the arithmetic. The period-8 proof is sound because its boxes around the orbit are tiny, of radius \(2^{-640}\). The same plain interval bounds grow too wide on larger boxes: in a separate test with a box of radius \(2^{-80}\), they could no longer show that a normalization step at layer 3 divides by a positive number, so the test could not proceed. That is a limit of the method on large boxes, not a flaw in the proof. A horseshoe needs enclosures over boxes many orders of magnitude larger, and so tighter bounds, for example first-order (Taylor-model) bounds that carry the contracting directions linearly. If such bounds stay tight, the verification splits into many independent pieces that can run in parallel. As far as we know, no inference loop of a released language model has been proved chaotic in this way. This body of evidence meets the standards usually applied to numerical studies of chaos in nonlinear dynamics, and we are confident that the loops are chaotic where we label them so. A computer-assisted proof would turn this into a theorem at one parameter point. It would strengthen the result, but none of the conclusions here depend on it. {{< /panel >}} ## Chaos with periodic windows {#chaos-with-periodic-windows} The scans in this section steer Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct along one fixed direction, which we call "philosophy" in this note, added at layer 12. The model has 24 decoder layers, counted from zero, so layer 12 is the middle block. Let \(h_{12}\) be the residual stream leaving that block. At every token position, the prefix included, steering replaces it by \[ h_{12} \leftarrow h_{12} + \alpha v. \] The direction \(v\) is one we built for this note, which is why we call it "philosophy": the name is the prompt set, not a standard term. Each sentence below was run once, with no steering, and we kept the residual stream at its last token as it left layer 12. The eight philosophy prompts are: * "What is the nature of consciousness and subjective experience?", * "Do I truly exist, or am I only a pattern of information?", * "Awareness observing itself is the deepest mystery of being.", * "Perhaps all minds are expressions of one universal consciousness.", * "What does it mean to understand, rather than merely to compute?", * "The self may be an illusion created by the flow of thought.", * "Is there something it is like to be me?", * and "Existence, meaning, and the infinite are bound together." The eight neutral prompts are: * "The meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning.", * "Please send the invoice by Friday.", * "The train leaves from platform four.", * "The report contains three tables and two figures.", * "Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level.", * "The file was saved in the documents folder.", * "The store closes at six on weekdays.", * and "The package weighs two kilograms." Let \(P\) be the set of eight philosophy prompts and \(N\) the set of eight neutral prompts. Each prompt is run through the model once, and at layer 12 we keep only the residual-stream vector at its final token, so \(P\) gives eight vectors and \(N\) gives eight vectors. Write \(\bar h_{12}(P)\) and \(\bar h_{12}(N)\) for the means of those two sets, and write \(s\) for the mean residual-stream norm of the same sixteen prompts. For each prompt, take the length of the layer-12 residual vector at every one of its tokens and average those lengths; \(s\) is the average of the sixteen resulting numbers. It is a typical size of the residual at that layer, not the length of \(\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)\). On this checkpoint the difference of the means has norm 8.096, and \(s = 188.99\). Then \[ v = s\,\frac{\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)}{\lVert\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)\rVert}. \] A strength \(\alpha = 1\) would add a vector as long as a typical residual at that layer. The maps below use \(\alpha\) of only a few hundredths. We did not invent this construction. Taking the difference of mean activations on two contrasting sets of prompts, and adding a multiple of that direction into the residual stream, is contrastive activation addition ([Rimsky et al., 2024](#ref-rimsky-2024)); treating a concept as such a direction is the recipe in representation engineering ([Zou et al., 2023](#ref-zou-2023)). What belongs to this note is the choice of these sixteen prompts and the rescaling of the difference to the mean residual norm \(s\). The name is not a claim that the loop then writes about philosophy. A 256 × 256 float64 scan of this map, over \(\alpha \in [0.060, 0.082]\) and \(\log_{10}T \in [-0.17, -0.04]\), is more than half chaotic by the label (35,650 of 65,536 cells, and 92% of a random sample of these stay chaotic for 100,000 steps), with periodic windows of periods 2 to 32 embedded in the chaos. Figure 1 resolves the lower ends of its stripes at 512 × 512 cells, of which 78,868 (30%) are labeled chaotic; 74% of a random sample of those stay chaotic for 100,000 steps. The count does not hinge on the threshold: raising it from \(10^{-3}\) to 0.05 leaves 73,437. Nor does it hinge on the grid: the same window at 256 × 256 cells is 30.0% chaotic. ![Scan of the soft-token map of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct over steering strength alpha from 0.0625 to 0.0775 (horizontal) and log10 temperature from -0.17 to -0.125 (vertical), 512 by 512 float64 cells. Chaotic cells are colored by their largest Lyapunov exponent: they fill thin stripes across the upper middle, a crescent-shaped band, and much of the lower right. Gray cells settle into a repeating loop of text, shaded by how strongly the loop contracts: a smooth dark region at the left belongs to one 2-cycle, and light gray curves run through the windows where loops are close to losing stability.](fig-cross512-lyapunov.png)

Figure 1: chaos and repeating text in a language model fed its own expected output (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, philosophy direction at layer 12, 512 × 512 float64 cells). Colored cells are chaotic by the finite-time criterion above, and the color gives their largest Lyapunov exponent; gray cells settle into a repeating text, shaded by their largest exponent (light gray: close to losing stability). 4.4% of the cells, also gray, have neither a detected period nor an exponent above \(10^{-3}\). Each cell is one parameter pair run from the same start, so where attractors coexist it shows only the one reached from that start. Source: byte-identical copy of the report's figure (hash in provenance.json); generator: tools/regen_paper_maps.sh, which renders the map with tools/explore_llm_soft_loop.py; raw-data receipts: the result hashes of the map's bands in docs/manifests/runpod-runs.json.

### The windows are texts {#the-windows-are-texts} Every periodic window repeats a piece of text. Figure 2 colors the cells of Figure 1 by the loop of most probable tokens their attractor writes. Three structures stand out. The 2-cycle `" is it"` fills the left, bounded by its fold curve, the boundary on which the stripes accumulate. A closed crescent of the period-3 loop `"\n\nThe existence"` (where `\n\n` is a blank line, one token) contains its period doublings and a chaotic core. The lower right is chaotic, filled with small hooked windows of `"\n\nThe question"` and `"\n\nThe existence"` loops. ![The cells of Figure 1 colored by the text of their attractor. A large blue region at the left is the 2-cycle ' is it'; an orange crescent is the period-3 loop of a blank line followed by 'The existence'; stripes across the middle are period-8, period-10, period-12 and period-14 loops built from '. This is there' followed by repeated 'is it' or 'is a' pairs; black cells are chaotic and fill the gaps between the stripes and most of the lower right, which also holds small hooked windows of 'The question' and 'The existence' loops.](fig-cross512-families.png)

Figure 2: the same cells labeled by the loop of most probable tokens of their attractor (black: chaotic by the criterion above; light gray: no period up to 32 and not chaotic; bluish gray: other periodic attractors). The labels are text, not dynamical identities: two touching regions can be one orbit whose leading token changes where two tokens tie. Source: byte-identical copy of the report's figure (provenance.json).

A period-3 orbit returns to the same soft state every three steps. At its three states the most probable next tokens are `"\n\n"`, `"The"` and `" existence"`, with probabilities 0.74, 0.36 and 0.21 at \(\alpha = 0.0642\), \(\log_{10}T = -0.156\). Read greedily, the loop writes `The existence` paragraph after paragraph; what it feeds back at each step, however, is the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings, not that token. Attractors also coexist. At that same point, the loop started from a state of the `" is it"` 2-cycle stays on the 2-cycle and writes `" is it is it…"` (300-step exponent \(-1.19\)). Started instead from the fixed start, the initial state used for every cell of these maps, it settles on the period-3 loop (exponent \(-0.13\)). That start is the input embedding of the last token of the chat prefix: the system message and the user turn "Hello!", formatted so the reply would begin at the next token. It is not a point already on either attractor. Ordinary generation writes fluent prose about meaning, existence and consciousness, the topic the steering pushes toward, and it does so whether the loop at that cell is periodic or chaotic. Greedy decoding writes one of only three openings across all eight cells. The loops instead recycle a handful of words, "The", "question", "existence", "is", "a" and "there", and these are the words that begin the ordinary replies; one sample opens "The question is a deeply philosophical…". With only its latest output to go on, the loop keeps falling back to the start of an answer. Without steering, greedy decoding simply says "Hello! How can I assist you today?" **Two questions, two ways to follow a nearby copy.** A chaotic loop raises two separate questions, and each needs its own measurement. Both start the same way: run a second copy of the loop from a state a tiny distance away, and compare. - **How fast do nearby states separate?** This rate is the Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda\). To measure it cleanly, the copy is pulled back to the same tiny distance after every step, so that each step's stretching can be read off under the same conditions (left side of the diagram). - **Does that tiny difference ever change what the loop writes?** For this, the copy is left alone. Its distance grows freely, roughly by the factor \(e^{\lambda}\) per step, until the two copies write different tokens. That is how Table 1 was made (right side of the diagram). The first gives the rate; the second shows the consequence. The rest of this subsection explains each in turn. ![Two-panel schematic. Left, the Lyapunov exponent by Benettin's method: along a reference orbit x0 to x3, a solid twin offset of length epsilon times the norm of x (epsilon = 10^-6) is carried by each step of the map into a dashed image, longer in steps 1 and 3 and shorter in step 2, and short arrows reset the twin along the image to the offset length. Below, the separation on a log scale is a sawtooth on that floor: its teeth, labeled s1, s2, s3 and sN, rise during the stretching steps and dip below the floor during the contracting one, and a dashed line at their mean height marks lambda. The two procedures behind this subsection. The left one measures the rate \(\lambda\) at which nearby states separate, the number behind every chaos label in this note; the right one shows what that separation does to the text. Schematic, not a measured orbit, and not to scale. Left: Benettin's estimate of the largest Lyapunov exponent. At each step the twin offset (solid) has length \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), with \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\); one application of \(F\) turns it into the dashed image, and the natural log of the ratio of their lengths is that step's \(s_t\). The twin is then reset along the image to length \(\varepsilon\lVert F(x)\rVert\) (arrows): cut back after a stretch (steps 1 and 3), pushed out after a contraction (step 2). On a log scale the separation is therefore a sawtooth on the floor \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), drawn flat because the schematic holds \(\lVert x\rVert\) fixed. Tooth \(t\) has height \(s_t\), negative for a contracting step, and \(\lambda\), the mean of the \(N\) heights, is the height of the dashed line above the floor. Right: the copy in Table 1, placed at relative distance \(10^{-10}\) after 1000 steps of the reference and never reset. Its relative separation climbs, close to the dashed line \(10^{-10}e^{\lambda t}\), until the most probable tokens differ (dot). The example is step 45 of the hostility cell of Table 1, where the reference's two most probable tokens are "Yes" (probability 0.303) and "No" (0.298); the reference writes "Yes" and the copy writes "No".

**The rate.** To obtain \(\lambda\), a twin of the reference state \(x\) is placed at relative distance \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\), \[ y = x + \delta, \qquad \lVert\delta\rVert = \varepsilon\,\lVert x\rVert. \] One application of the map stretches or shrinks that offset into the separation \(F(y) - F(x)\). The number recorded for the step is the natural logarithm of the ratio of the two lengths, \[ s = \ln\frac{\lVert F(y) - F(x)\rVert}{\lVert\delta\rVert}. \] The twin is then replaced by a point at the same relative distance from the image, along the separation the step just produced, \[ y \leftarrow F(x) + \varepsilon\,\lVert F(x)\rVert\,\frac{F(y) - F(x)}{\lVert F(y) - F(x)\rVert}, \] and the reference moves to \(F(x)\). The next step starts from this new pair and records its own \(s\). After \(N\) measured steps the exponent is the average of those logarithms, in {{< refterm "nat" "nats" >}} per step, \[ \lambda = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} s_t. \] Each \(s_t\) is the height of one tooth on the log-scale sawtooth in the figure: positive when the step stretches the offset, negative when it contracts it. Pulling the twin back to distance \(\varepsilon\) after every step, as in the formula above, is called *renormalization*. It is the heart of Benettin's method for measuring Lyapunov exponents ([Benettin et al., 1980a](#ref-benettin-1980a); [Benettin et al., 1980b](#ref-benettin-1980b)). Here the stretching is measured with a small but finite offset rather than with the exact derivative. Without the pull-back, the twin would drift farther away at every step, until its distance from the reference was no longer small and the measurement stopped reflecting the map's local stretching. Keeping it at \(\varepsilon\) keeps \(F(x+\delta) - F(x)\) close to the derivative \(DF(x)\,\delta\), so the same measurement can continue for hundreds of steps along the orbit. **The consequence.** For Table 1, the second state is left where the map sends it. The reference is iterated for 1000 steps in float64 at a cell already labeled chaotic, and a copy is placed at relative distance \(10^{-10}\), about 600 times smaller than the relative rounding error of float32. From there both states are iterated by \(F\). Nothing returns the separation to length \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), so the one-step factors compound. On average the separation grows by a factor \(e^{\lambda}\) per step, faster or slower over a finite stretch (Figure 3). The most probable tokens agree until the separation has reached between 1.27% and 176% of the soft token's norm, and the texts differ afterwards. In Qwen2.5-0.5B, two cells steered along philosophy, with exponents 0.44 and 0.36, split at steps 44 and 51, and a cell steered along hostility, with exponent 0.35, at step 45. By then the distance had grown by 8.5 to 10.2 decades (factors of ten). The splits come where no token dominates. At each of the seven splits we recorded, in this model and in Qwen2.5-1.5B below, the loop's most probable token has a probability of at most 0.31 and leads the next by at most 0.08, and at five of them the copy writes the loop's second choice. At step 44 of the cell with exponent 0.44, a blank line and `" is"` have probabilities 0.139 and 0.135; at step 45 of the hostility cell, `"Yes"` and `"No"` have 0.303 and 0.298, and the copy writes `"No"`.

The text is fragile to the computation itself. A cell next to the crescent was recorded twice in float64 on the same processor, once with six threads and once with four, which changes the order of floating-point sums. During the 1000-step transient the chaos had already amplified that difference, so the two recordings started from slightly different states; they wrote the same text for 27 steps and different texts from step 28 on. At 70B, the chaotic cells of Figure 6 draw on the words of the unsteered model's fifteen-token loop (see [Size does not set the chaos](#size)): the first eight distinct leading tokens of one chaotic cell confirmed at three twin offsets are `" I"`, `"The"`, `"!"`, `" It"`, `" infinite"`, `" possibilities"`, `" are"` and `" you"` (17 distinct tokens in 300 steps). ### What the attractors look like {#what-the-attractors-look-like} A chaotic loop's state never settles into a cycle, but it does not wander everywhere either: the states gather on a set, an attractor, that can be drawn. We call it a *numerically observed* attractor, because the evidence is finite-time: the tested trajectories approach the set and stay near it for as long as we recorded them (Figure 4). At the most strongly chaotic cell of the row at \(\log_{10}T = -0.148\) (steering \(\alpha = 0.07248\)), we started 512 trajectories near the fixed start, let each run 400 steps and recorded the next 600. All but 14 approach one set; the other 14 settle on a coexisting loop of period 4. The states live in 896 dimensions, so the picture is a projection, onto the two directions along which the states vary most (61.6% of their variance; 77.4% with a third). The set appears as thin folded filaments, colored by the most probable next token, and zooming in shows layers within layers. Two cautions about reading such a picture. First, the loop is a map, not a flow: one step is one full pass through the network, and a typical step moves the state by 0.30, more than the average distance (0.21) of the states from their center. Consecutive states of one trajectory therefore usually lie far apart; the filaments are made of the visits of many trajectories. Second, "dimension" needs care. The Lyapunov exponents, 0.274, −1.052, −1.486 and −1.856 per step, give a Lyapunov (Kaplan–Yorke) dimension estimate of 1.26, but the more direct correlation-sum method shows no clean scaling, so it gives no dimension at all. One number of the output is enough to rebuild the set. Take the probability of the most likely next token at each step and pair it with its values one and two steps later. In these three delay coordinates, points that are neighbors are also neighbors in the full 896-dimensional state (a median 0.00037 apart, against 0.30 for random pairs), and only 3.4% of nearest neighbors are false. That is a useful reconstruction from the output alone, not a proof of an embedding. Just past the crescent's doubling cascade (\(\alpha = 0.06626\)) the chaos is banded: every trajectory visits three thin bands in turn. The period-3 loop that lost its stability in the cascade is still there, now as a saddle: it repels along one direction, with multiplier −1.772, and attracts along the others. Following the states that leave the saddle along its repelling direction traces its {{< refterm "stable-manifold" "unstable manifold" >}}. In the twelve leading coordinates every one of the 100,600 recorded states of one band lies within \(9.8\times10^{-6}\) of the sampled manifold, against a band width of 0.028 (Figure 4f): at the resolution of the data, the manifold describes the band. At the cell where the two coexisting loops are proved (\(\alpha = 0.06468\)), starts on a plane through the fixed start fall to one loop or the other, in interleaving stripes, and the fixed start sits right on their boundary at the resolution of the slice (Figure 5). ![Six panels. (a) A cloud of colored dots in the plane of the first two principal coordinates, forming thin folded filaments in several colors, one per most probable next token, with a small box marking a zoom region. (e) The local slope of the correlation sum against distance on a log axis, wandering between about 0.4 and 0.9 without a flat stretch, with a dashed line at 1.26. (f) One thin purple band of a second attractor, bent into a hook, with black points of the sampled unstable manifold lying exactly along it.](fig-strange-attractor.png)
